analysis.investment_thesis: Firstsource trades at INR 239 vs. a Graham Number of ~INR 110 (computed from EPS ~₹8.6 and BVPS ~₹63), meaning the market demands a 117% premium over my intrinsic value estimate with no margin of safety whatsoever. With P/E at 24.1x and P/B at 3.78x — both more than double my maximum thresholds — Mr. Market is pricing in optimism I am unwilling to pay for.
key_strengths: 9+ consecutive years of positive net profit (2016–2025) — the minimum earnings continuity I demand
Revenue and operating income both growing steadily (10.6% and 13.4% CAGR over 9 years) with no loss years
Promoter holding of 53.66% and strong DII interest (25.49%) indicate institutional confidence in the business
key_risks: Valuation is the dominant risk: P/E 24.1x and P/B 3.78x leave zero margin of safety by any Graham standard
Debt surged sharply in FY2025 (borrowings +55% YoY to ₹2,369 Cr) while cash nearly evaporated (₹69 Cr → ₹13 Cr) — a dangerous combination
Finance costs compounding at 13.1% CAGR, outpacing net profit growth of 9.6% — earnings quality is being eroded by leverage
red_flags: Graham Number ~₹110 vs. price ₹239 — stock trades at 2.17x intrinsic value estimate
Debt/Equity of 0.54 breaches my 0.5 ceiling; FY2025 debt jump of ₹1,043 Cr with no disclosed acquisition rationale is unexplained
Free cash flow declining from ₹806 Cr (FY21) to ₹477 Cr (FY25) even as revenue grew 57% over the same period — FCF conversion is deteriorating
Near-zero cash of ₹13 Cr against ₹2,569 Cr total debt provides minimal liquidity buffer
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Applying my quantitative filters, Firstsource fails on every valuation metric I use. A P/E of 24.1x is 60% above my absolute ceiling of 15x; P/B of 3.78x is more than twice my 1.5x limit. The Graham Number — the square root of (22.5 × ₹8.59 EPS × ₹63.1 BVPS) — yields approximately ₹110, against a market price of ₹239. The intelligent investor does not pay a 117% premium over the arithmetic of the balance sheet. The business itself is respectable: nine years of unbroken profits, modest but consistent revenue compounding, and a 15% ROE. But respectability and cheapness are different things entirely.

What troubles me further is the balance sheet deterioration in FY2025. Borrowings jumped from ₹1,526 Cr to ₹2,369 Cr — a ₹843 Cr increase — while cash fell from ₹69 Cr to ₹13 Cr, and investing outflows reached ₹744 Cr. Finance costs are now ₹184 Cr annually and growing at 13.1% compounded, faster than net profit. Free cash flow has declined from ₹806 Cr in FY21 to ₹477 Cr in FY25 even as revenues expanded significantly — meaning the business is absorbing capital faster than it is generating it. I would require the price to fall near the Graham Number (roughly ₹110–₹120) before this stock entered my circle of consideration.
